hints: Focus on what a catalyst does, it gets used up in one step and then must be remade in a later step.
Notice that $\text{NO}_2$ is the oxidising catalyst here, so it oxidises $\text{SO}_2$ to $\text{SO}_3$ while itself is reduced to $\text{NO}$.
Look for the reaction that starts with $\text{NO}$ and turns it back into $\text{NO}_2$ using oxygen from the air.
walkthrough:
**Recall the catalytic step**

Think of $\text{NO}_2$ as the helper. It gives an oxygen atom to sulfur dioxide.

Chemical equation for the catalysed oxidation:
$$\text{SO}_2 + \text{NO}_2 \rightarrow \text{SO}_3 + \text{NO}$$

**Spot what needs regenerating**

After Step 1 the catalyst $\text{NO}_2$ has become $\text{NO}$. A catalyst is not used up overall, so $\text{NO}$ must be converted back to $\text{NO}_2$.

This is the definition of regeneration: remake the original catalyst.

**Add oxygen to remake the catalyst**

In the atmosphere there is plenty of $\text{O}_2$ to re-oxidise $\text{NO}$ back to $\text{NO}_2$.

Regeneration equation:
$$\text{NO} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{NO}_2$$

options.A: Shows direct combination of $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ to $\text{NO}_2$. This is not the second step of the cycle because it does not start from $\text{NO}$, so it does not remake $\text{NO}_2$ from the reduced product.
options.B: This is the catalytic oxidation of ammonia in the Ostwald process to make $\text{NO}$. It is an industrial preparation of $\text{NO}$, not the atmospheric regeneration of $\text{NO}_2$ from $\text{NO}$.
options.C: This shows formation of $\text{NO}$ from $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ at high temperature, for example in lightning. It makes $\text{NO}$, but it does not convert $\text{NO}$ back to the $\text{NO}_2$ catalyst.
options.D: This is exactly the regeneration step. The $\text{NO}$ formed when $\text{NO}_2$ oxidised $\text{SO}_2$ is re-oxidised by atmospheric $\text{O}_2$ back to $\text{NO}_2$, so the $\text{NO}_2$ catalyst is restored and the cycle can continue.
